danish.title: Ottende bog (1811–12) — Kapitel 14
paragraphs: Morgenen kom med sine gøremål og sin travlhed. Alle stod op og begyndte at gå rundt og tale, syerskerne kom igen. Marja Dmitrijevna viste sig, og de blev kaldt til morgenmad. Natasja blev ved med uroligt at se på alle med vidåbne øjne, som om hun ville opfange hvert blik rettet mod hende, og forsøgte at fremstå som sædvanligt.
Efter morgenmaden, som var hendes bedste tid, satte Marja Dmitrijevna sig i sin lænestol og kaldte Natasja og greven til sig.

»Nå, venner, nu har jeg tænkt hele sagen igennem, og her er mit råd,« begyndte hun. »I går, som I ved, tog jeg hen til fyrst Bolkonskij. Nå, jeg havde en samtale med ham... Han fandt på at begynde at råbe, men mig råber man ikke ned. Jeg sagde, hvad jeg havde at sige!«
»Nå, og han?« spurgte greven.

»Han? Han er vanvittig... han ville ikke høre efter. Men hvad nytter det at snakke? Som det er, har vi slidt den stakkels pige op,« sagde Marja Dmitrijevna. »Mit råd til jer er: gør jeres forretninger færdige og tag hjem til Otradnoje... og vent der.«
»Åh, nej!« udbrød Natasja.
»Jo, tag hjem,« sagde Marja Dmitrijevna, »og vent der. Hvis din forlovede kommer her nu — kan et skænderi ikke undgås; men alene med den gamle mand kan han tale tingene igennem og så komme til jer.«

Grev Rostov bifaldt dette forslag og værdsatte dets fornuft. Hvis den gamle mand ændrede sind, ville det være endnu bedre at besøge ham i Moskva eller på Lysye Gory senere; og hvis ikke, kunne brylluppet, mod hans ønske, kun arrangeres på Otradnoje.
»Det er helt rigtigt. Og jeg er ked af, at jeg tog derhen og bragte hende med,« sagde den gamle greve.

»Nej, hvorfor være ked af det? Når I nu er her, måtte I jo hilse på ham. Men hvis han ikke vil — det er hans sag,« sagde Marja Dmitrijevna og ledte efter noget i sin taske. »Desuden er udstyret klar, så der er intet at vente på; og hvad der ikke er klar, sender jeg efter jer. Selvom jeg nødig lader jer tage af sted, er det det bedste. Så tag af sted, med Guds velsignelse!«
Da hun havde fundet det, hun ledte efter i tasken, rakte hun det til Natasja. Det var et brev fra fyrstinde Marja.
»Hun har skrevet til dig. Hvor hun plager sig selv, den stakkel! Hun er bange for, at du tror, hun ikke kan lide dig.«
»Men hun kan ikke lide mig,« sagde Natasja.
»Snak ikke vrøvl!« udbrød Marja Dmitrijevna.

»Jeg tror ikke på nogen, jeg ved, hun ikke kan lide mig,« svarede Natasja frimodigt, idet hun tog brevet, og hendes ansigt udtrykte en kold og vred beslutsomhed, der fik Marja Dmitrijevna til at se nærmere på hende og rynke bryn.
»Svar ikke sådan, min gode pige!« sagde hun. »Hvad jeg siger, er sandt! Skriv et svar!«
Natasja svarede ikke og gik ind på sit værelse for at læse fyrstinde Marjas brev.

Fyrstinde Marja skrev, at hun var fortvivlet over den misforståelse, der var opstået mellem dem. Uanset hendes fars følelser bad hun Natasja tro, at hun kun kunne elske hende som den, hendes bror havde valgt, for hvis lykke hun var rede til at ofre alt.

»Tro dog ikke,« skrev hun, »at min far er uvenligt stemt mod dig. Han er syg og gammel og må tilgives; men han er god og storstilet og vil komme til at elske den, der gør hans søn lykkelig.« Fyrstinde Marja bad desuden Natasja fastsætte et tidspunkt, hvor de kunne ses igen.

Efter at have læst brevet satte Natasja sig ved skrivebordet for at svare. »Kære fyrstinde,« skrev hun hurtigt og mekanisk på fransk og holdt så inde. Hvad mere kunne hun skrive efter alt, hvad der var sket aftenen før? »Ja, ja! Alt det er sket, og nu er alt forandret,« tænkte hun, mens hun sad med det påbegyndte brev foran sig. »Er jeg nødt til at bryde med ham? Er jeg det virkelig? Det er forfærdeligt...« Og for at flygte fra disse frygtelige tanker gik hun hen til Sonja og gav sig til at sortere mønstre med hende.

Efter middag gik Natasja ind på sit værelse og tog igen fyrstinde Marjas brev frem. »Kan det virkelig alt sammen være forbi?« tænkte hun. »Kan det virkelig være, at alt dette er sket så hurtigt og har ødelagt alt det, der var før?« Hun genkaldte sig sin kærlighed til fyrst Andrej i al dens tidligere styrke og følte samtidig, at hun elskede Kuragin. Hun forestillede sig tydeligt som fyrst Andrejs hustru med alle de lykkedrømme, hun så ofte havde gentaget i sin fantasi, og på samme tid, glødende af ophidselse, genkaldte hun sig hver eneste detalje fra gårsdagens møde med Anatole.

»Hvorfor kunne det ikke også lade sig gøre?« spurgte hun sig selv til tider i fuldstændig forvirring. »Kun sådan kunne jeg være helt lykkelig; men nu er jeg nødt til at vælge, og jeg kan ikke være lykkelig uden nogen af dem. Blot,« tænkte hun, »at fortælle fyrst Andrej, hvad der er sket, eller skjule det for ham er begge dele lige umuligt. Men med ham er intet ødelagt. Men skal jeg virkelig for altid opgive glæden ved fyrst Andrejs kærlighed, som jeg har levet i så længe?«
»Frøken!« hviskede en tjenestepige, der trådte ind i rummet med hemmelighedsfuld mine. »En mand bad mig give Dem dette —« og hun rakte Natasja et brev.

»Bare, for Kristi skyld...« fortsatte pigen, da Natasja uden at tænke mekanisk brød seglet og læste et kærlighedsbrev fra Anatole, som hun, uden at fatte et eneste ord, kun forstod var et brev fra ham — fra den mand, hun elskede. Ja, hun elskede ham, for hvordan kunne det, der var sket, ellers være sket? Og hvordan kunne hun have et kærlighedsbrev fra ham i sin hånd?
Med skælvende hænder holdt Natasja det lidenskabelige kærlighedsbrev, som Dolokhov havde skrevet for Anatole, og idet hun læste det, fandt hun deri et ekko af alt det, hun selv indbildte sig at føle.

»Siden i går aftes er min skæbne beseglet; at blive elsket af dig eller dø. Der er ingen anden vej for mig,« begyndte brevet. Derpå sagde han, at han vidste, hendes forældre ikke ville give hende til ham — hertil var der hemmelige grunde, som han kun kunne åbenbare for hende — men hvis hun elskede ham, behøvede hun blot at sige ja, og ingen menneskelig magt kunne hindre deres lykke. Kærligheden ville overvinde alt. Han ville bortføre hende og bringe hende til verdens ende.
»Ja, ja! Jeg elsker ham!« tænkte Natasja, da hun læste brevet for tyvende gang og fandt en særlig dyb mening i hvert eneste ord.
Den aften skulle Marja Dmitrijevna til familien Akharov og foreslog at tage pigerne med. Natasja, der undskyldte sig med hovedpine, blev hjemme.

english.title: Book Eight (1811 - 12) — Chapter 14
paragraphs: Morning came with its cares and bustle. Everyone got up and began to move about and talk, dressmakers came again. Marya Dmitrievna appeared, and they were called to breakfast. Natasha kept looking uneasily at everybody with wide-open eyes, as if trying to intercept every glance directed at her, and tried to appear the same as usual.
After breakfast, which was her best time, Marya Dmitrievna settled into her armchair and called Natasha and the count over.

"Well, friends, I've now thought the whole matter over and this is my advice," she began. "Yesterday, as you know, I went to see Prince Bolkonsky. Well, I had a talk with him... He got it into his head to start shouting, but I'm not one to be shouted down. I said what I had to say!"
"Well, and he?" asked the count.

"He? He's out of his mind... he wouldn't listen. But what's the use of talking? As it is, we've worn the poor girl out," said Marya Dmitrievna. "My advice to you is: finish your business and go back home to Otradnoe... and wait there."
"Oh, no!" exclaimed Natasha.
"Yes, go back," said Marya Dmitrievna, "and wait there. If your fiance comes here now there'll be no avoiding a quarrel; but alone with the old man he'll talk things over and then come on to you."

Count Rostov approved of this suggestion, seeing its good sense. If the old man came around, it would be even better to visit him in Moscow or at Bald Hills later; and if not, the wedding, against his wishes, could only be arranged at Otradnoe.
"That's exactly right. And I'm sorry I went to see him and took her," said the old count.

"No, why be sorry? Being here, you had to pay your respects. But if he won't — that's his business," said Marya Dmitrievna, looking for something in her handbag. "Besides, the trousseau is ready, so there's nothing to wait for; and what's not ready I'll send after you. Though I don't like letting you go, it's the best thing. So go, with God's blessing!"
Having found what she was looking for in the handbag, she handed it to Natasha. It was a letter from Princess Mary.
"She's written to you. How she torments herself, poor thing! She's afraid you might think she doesn't like you."
"But she doesn't like me," said Natasha.
"Don't talk nonsense!" cried Marya Dmitrievna.

"I won't believe anyone — I know she doesn't like me," replied Natasha boldly as she took the letter, and her face expressed a cold and angry determination that caused Marya Dmitrievna to look at her more closely and frown.
"Don't answer like that, my good girl!" she said. "What I say is true! Write an answer!"
Natasha didn't reply and went to her own room to read Princess Mary's letter.

Princess Mary wrote that she was in despair at the misunderstanding between them. Whatever her father's feelings might be, she begged Natasha to believe that she could not help loving her as the one chosen by her brother, for whose happiness she was ready to sacrifice everything.

"Do not think, however," she wrote, "that my father is ill-disposed toward you. He is an invalid and an old man who must be forgiven; but he is good and generous and will love the woman who makes his son happy." Princess Mary went on to ask Natasha to set a time when she could see her again.

After reading the letter, Natasha sat down at the writing table to answer it. "Dear Princess," she wrote quickly and mechanically in French, and then paused. What more could she write after everything that had happened the evening before? "Yes, yes! All that has happened, and now everything is changed," she thought as she sat with the unfinished letter before her. "Must I break off with him? Must I really? That's awful..." and to escape from these dreadful thoughts she went to Sonya and began sorting patterns with her.

After dinner Natasha went to her room and again took up Princess Mary's letter. "Can it really be all over?" she thought. "Can it be that all this has happened so quickly and has destroyed everything that went before?" She recalled her love for Prince Andrew in all its former strength, and at the same time felt that she loved Kuragin. She vividly pictured herself as Prince Andrew's wife, and the scenes of happiness with him she had imagined so often, and at the same time, glowing with excitement, recalled every detail of yesterday's encounter with Anatole.

"Why couldn't that be as well?" she sometimes asked herself in complete bewilderment. "Only that way could I be completely happy; but now I have to choose, and I can't be happy without either of them. Only," she thought, "to tell Prince Andrew what has happened or to hide it from him are both equally impossible. But with that one nothing is ruined. But am I really to give up forever the joy of Prince Andrew's love, in which I've lived so long?"
"Please, Miss!" whispered a maid, entering the room with a mysterious air. "A man told me to give you this—" and she handed Natasha a letter.

"Only, for Christ's sake..." the girl went on, as Natasha, without thinking, mechanically broke the seal and read a love letter from Anatole, of which, without taking in a word, she understood only that it was a letter from him — from the man she loved. Yes, she loved him, or else how could what had happened have happened? And how could she have a love letter from him in her hand?
With trembling hands Natasha held that passionate love letter which Dolokhov had composed for Anatole, and as she read it she found in it an echo of everything she imagined she herself was feeling.

"Since yesterday evening my fate has been sealed; to be loved by you or to die. There is no other way for me," the letter began. Then he went on to say that he knew her parents would not give her to him — for this there were secret reasons he could reveal only to her — but that if she loved him she need only say the word yes, and no human power could prevent their happiness. Love would conquer all. He would steal her away and carry her off to the ends of the earth.
"Yes, yes! I love him!" thought Natasha, reading the letter for the twentieth time and finding some especially deep meaning in each word of it.
That evening Marya Dmitrievna was going to the Akharovs' and proposed to take the girls with her. Natasha, pleading a headache, stayed home.
